extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; early-18th-century literate public interested in essays, moral reflections, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A page from The Spectator (early 18th-century periodical) containing short essays, fictional letters, allegorical visions (the mountain of the Muses), moral and political reflections. It is literary and rhetorical rather than an explicit how-to or guideline document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for poetic inspiration (Solitude, Silence, Contemplation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solitude is represented as a place whose only admitted companions are 'Silence' and 'Contemplation'; before Solitude lay a 'celestial Globe, with several Schemes of Mathematical Theorems.' The Grove was originally 'designed for... those whom the Study and Love of Wisdom had fitted for divine Conversation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage presents solitude, silence, and contemplation (together with study) as the proper dispositions and preparation for access to the Muses and poetic inspiration. The Grove rewards lives 'according to the Dictates of their Conscience and the Commands of the Gods,' implying inward seriousness and study are prerequisites for true poetic/musical elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two paths to poetic eminence: Genius (birth) vs Diligence (work)
rubrics_metrics.description: There were two Paths... the one was guarded by the Genius which presides over the Moment of our Births (admitting only those on whom Melpomene had look'd propitiously); the other Way was guarded by Diligence, 'so tedious in granting their Request, and indeed after Admittance the Way was so very intricate and laborious, that many... chose rather to return back.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats poetic success as attainable either by innate genius (rare, immediate admission) or by long, labourious diligence (accessible but arduous); it also depicts a third path combining both, which carries 'those happy Few' directly to Apollo. This functions as a normative claim about routes to literary achievement: talent can admit quickly, but sustained labour is a valid (though difficult) alternative; the ideal is a blend of both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit arises from a balance of Fancy and Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy is described as a nymph 'continually varying her Dress' and sometimes 'into the most wild and freakish Garb,' while Judgment, 'of great Gravity,' 'corrected her Inconsistences... and still flung her affected and unbecoming Ornaments down the Mountain.' Between them sat a youth named 'Wit,' 'their genuine Offspring.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The allegory prescribes a compositional principle for literary taste: imagination (Fancy) must be tempered and corrected by taste and restraint (Judgment); properly combined they produce Wit. Examples/anti-patterns: unchecked fancy produces inconsistency and affectation; purely judgment without fancy would lack vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of revision/authorization by the Muses (editorial oversight)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator observes 'Boccalini sending Dispatches to the World below of what happened upon Parnassus; but I perceived he did it without leave of the Muses, and by stealth, and was unwilling to have them revised by Apollo.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicitly recommends that literary/material for public dissemination should undergo the Muses'/Apollo's revision—i.e., proper editorial review or sanction—rather than being published hastily or without approval. The anti-pattern is unauthorized or furtive publishing that avoids revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coquetry and social artifice as practiced technique (affectation as charm)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a letter from a coquette: 'That our greatest Charms are owing to Affectation... 'Tis to Affectation we owe the pensive Attention of Deidamia at a Tragedy... and the lowly Aspect of Lanquicelsa at a Sermon.' The writer describes strategies: mortify a rival by favouring an insignificant creature, arrange dances so rivals suffer, cultivate a circle of obsequious admirers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although presented as a character sketch/letter, the passage lays out explicit social techniques and maxims for coquettish behaviour: use affectation deliberately to create charm, manipulate displays of favour to mortify rivals, orchestrate public scenes (dances, church, court) to secure admiration. The counterpoint in the reply emphasizes a conventional view that such gallantries aim ultimately at marriage and motherhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good monarch or ruler (moderation, service, integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between two rivals: one 'animated with a restless Desire of Glory' who pursues empire; the other seeks 'their rational and voluntary Obedience' and 'is delighted only with the Cause and Foundation of it to cherish and protect 'em.' The good prince is 'educated by Adversity,' has 'Integrity,' 'a quick Sense of the Distresses and Miseries of Mankind,' and rules by address rather than invasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This political-moral standard prescribes that a virtuous ruler should value the welfare and voluntary obedience of subjects over conquest and ostentation; be moderate, compassionate, and formed by trial; avoid hypocrisy (religion as mere disguise) and use power to 'relieve the Oppressed.' These claims serve as evaluative criteria for judging princes and statesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against religion as hypocrisy (religion must be sincere motive, not disguise)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Religion is but a convenient Disguise' is presented as the cynical Machiavellian scheme by which a prince might seem virtuous while serving his own interests; by contrast, genuine religion provides 'a vigorous Motive of Action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contains a normative principle: piety and religion must be authentic to be morally valuable; when religion is used as a mask for ambition it corrupts public life. This functions as a standard for evaluating claims of religious motivation in politics and leadership.
